baptism.question: What does the Bible say about baptism?
baptism.intro: Baptism is the rite with water in which Christ's followers are baptized, in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19) or in the name of Jesus Christ (Acts 2:38). Among the churches whose readings are set out here, all agree that Christ commanded it, and they read the text differently on who is to be baptized, on what baptism gives or shows, and, on a separate question, on how the water is applied. This page sets the main readings side by side, each in the words its holders use, and chooses none of them.

readings.label: Baptism as God's act of cleansing and new birth, given to believers and to the children of believers
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the New Testament to speak of baptism as the act in which God forgives sin, gives new birth and the Spirit, and joins a person to Christ and his church, so that texts such as Acts 2:38 and Titus 3:5 name what baptism itself does. They baptize infants as well as converts, taking the promise of Acts 2:39 and the household baptisms to include children. Catholic teaching speaks of the sacrament as working by Christ's act and not by the worth of the minister, counts baptism with water in the Trinitarian name in other churches as valid and not to be repeated (Catechism 1271-1272), names triple immersion the most expressive way and accepts pouring (Catechism 1239). Eastern Orthodox practice is threefold immersion (Longer Catechism, questions 288-290), joined with anointing (chrismation) and communion, normally in infancy; the Longer Catechism grounds infant baptism in the faith of parents and sponsors and in baptism's taking the place of circumcision (Colossians 2:11-12). Lutheran teaching holds baptism valid by God's word whether or not the recipient believes, and faith the means by which its gifts are received (Large Catechism, on Baptism). Anglican teaching holds part of this reading together with the second: the Church of England's Article XXVII calls baptism a sign of regeneration or new birth, by which, as by an instrument (a means), those who receive it rightly are grafted into the Church, and also says the promises of forgiveness and adoption are visibly signed and sealed, language that the second reading shares. Wesleyan and Methodist members hold it in part: the Articles of Religion held by the United Methodist Church (Article XVII) call baptism a sign of regeneration or new birth, and its statement By Water and the Spirit calls baptism the means of entry into new life in Christ; the same statement holds that the new birth may not always happen at the moment of baptism, and that the sacrament is received once, and John Wesley taught in Standard Sermon 45, on the new birth, that baptism is not itself the new birth, while noting that the Church of England supposes those baptized in infancy to be born again at the same time.

readings.label: Baptism as the sign and seal of God's covenant promise, given to believers and to their children
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take baptism to be the New Testament's sign of the covenant God made with Abraham and his descendants, as circumcision was its sign (Colossians 2:11-12). What baptism shows is washing, union with Christ and the Spirit's work; what it seals is God's promise, which faith receives. They baptize infants as well as converts, taking the promise to “you and your children” (Acts 2:39) and the household baptisms to follow Genesis 17, where the sign was given to every male of the household, infants on the eighth day among them. Reformed teaching calls baptism a sign and seal, baptizes the infants of one or both believing parents (Westminster Confession 28.4), and holds that the Spirit gives what it signifies as God wills. Anglican teaching holds part of this reading together with the first: Article XXVII speaks of the promises of forgiveness and adoption as visibly signed and sealed and keeps the baptism of young children, and the catechism of the Anglican Church in North America calls infant baptism a sign of the covenant promise; these documents do not link baptism to Abraham's covenant and circumcision, or speak of the Spirit giving what baptism signifies as God wills. United Methodist teaching (By Water and the Spirit) calls the baptism of infants and adults the sign of the covenant, as circumcision was the sign of the older covenant; Wesleyan and Methodist members also baptize adult converts, and some hold the first reading as well. The Westminster Confession names pouring or sprinkling and says dipping of the person is not necessary (28.3), and United Methodist teaching accepts sprinkling, pouring or immersion.

readings.label: Baptism of those who believe: obedience to Christ's command and a public answer to the gospel
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the New Testament's baptisms to follow hearing the gospel, believing and repenting, so that baptism belongs to those who profess faith in Christ, as in Acts 2:41 and Acts 8:12. They take baptism to picture the believer's union with Christ's death and rising (Romans 6:4), to be the believer's public answer to the gospel, and to be a step into the life of the church. Baptist and free-church readers call it an ordinance, a rite Christ commanded and his followers obey, and speak of grace received before baptism and shown in it. Southern Baptists (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, Article VII) make baptism a prerequisite to the privileges of church membership and to the Lord's Supper. Pentecostal churches share this practice: the Church of God and the Foursquare Church name the threefold name in their statements, the Assemblies of God statement cites Matthew 28:19, and Oneness Pentecostal bodies baptize in the name of Jesus alone, on Acts 2:38. Pentecostal churches distinguish baptism in water from what they call baptism in the Spirit, with members differing on what water baptism itself gives; Charismatic members within other traditions follow the practice of those traditions. Anabaptist readers (a name given by their opponents in the sixteenth century, meaning those who baptize again; they hold that the baptism they had received as infants was not baptism) speak of baptism as a pledge to follow Christ within the community. Anabaptist members differ on how baptism relates to grace, and the Mennonite and Schleitheim documents cited here state that baptism is for those who profess faith, but do not speak of a picture of Christ's death and rising. The 1995 Mennonite confession calls baptism a sign and speaks of being baptized into Christ and his body by the Spirit, water and blood, the last being the offering of one's life, the commitment to love enemies and renounce violence. On the mode, the Baptist Faith and Message 2000 describes baptism as the immersion of a believer and the 1689 London Confession calls immersion necessary to its due administration; the Assemblies of God and the Church of God name immersion; the Mennonite confession accepts pouring, immersion or sprinkling.

can-salvation-be-lost.question: What does the Bible say about whether salvation can be lost?
can-salvation-be-lost.intro: Christians ask whether a person who has been saved can lose that salvation, and they read the New Testament as holding promises that those who are Christ's are kept beside warnings that some turn away and are cut off. This page sets the main readings side by side, each in the words its holders use, and chooses none of them. The passages come from several New Testament writers, and readers differ on whether they hold one view or speak to different situations.

readings.label: Falling away is possible: the warnings address people who have been saved, and the one who remains in Christ is kept
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the warnings of Hebrews, John 15 and the letters of Paul to be addressed to people who have received salvation, and take them to mean that a person who has been saved can turn away and be lost, and that the one who remains in Christ is kept. Catholic teaching holds that the life of grace is lost by what is called mortal sin and is restored through repentance (Catechism 1855-1861; Council of Trent, Session 6, chapter 14); it also holds that faith can remain after grace is lost by mortal sin, and urges firm hope in God's help while denying certainty of final perseverance (Council of Trent, Session 6, chapters 13 and 15). Eastern Orthodox readers speak of a freedom to turn from God that stays with a person through life, and of salvation as a way walked to its end; the Confession of Dositheus (1672) holds that a baptized person who falls is restored through repentance and the Church's penance. Wesleyan and Methodist readers hold that a believer who turns from Christ can fall from grace and can return: the Articles of Religion of the United Methodist Church (Article XII) say that repentance is not to be denied to those who sin after justification, and the Global Methodist Church names the Articles of Religion among its doctrinal standards, and the United Methodist Confession of Faith (Article IX) says that it is possible to depart from grace and fall into sin; Wesley's sermon A Call to Backsliders teaches that those who have fallen from grace can be restored. The Assemblies of God states this reading in its bylaws and position paper (salvation may be abandoned by willfully turning from Christ, while the believer is secure in a living relationship with him), and members of Pentecostal churches of the Wesleyan holiness line share it. The National Association of Free Will Baptists says in its Treatise (chapter XIII) that the truly regenerate are in danger of falling and are to watch and pray lest they be lost; General Baptist readers hold this reading, and differ from the Baptist readers below on whether a believer can fall away. Lutheran teaching holds that a believer can fall from faith (the Formula of Concord, Epitome IV, rejects the teaching that faith and the Holy Spirit are not lost by wilful sin), that God keeps believers in faith through his word and sacraments, and that a person who has fallen away is brought back by the word of forgiveness (Augsburg Confession XII); Lutheran readers take assurance to rest on the promise of that word, and differ from Reformed readers on whether those who believe can fall away. Anabaptist readers hold that the warnings are addressed to the gathered church of believers: the Dordrecht Confession (1632, Article XVI) speaks of a church member who sins unto death and so forfeits the kingdom of God, the 1995 Mennonite confession (Article 14) treats church discipline as a sign of God's offer of forgiveness to believers who drift from faithful discipleship, and the same confession holds faith and faithful obedience to be inseparable (Article 8). The Church of England's Article XVI holds that after receiving the Holy Spirit a person may depart from grace given and, by God's grace, rise again; Anglican members differ on how far that stands beside Article XVII.

readings.label: The perseverance of the saints (the Calvinist, or Reformed, reading): God keeps those he has saved to the end, and the warnings are among the means he uses to keep them
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the New Testament to teach that those God has saved are kept in faith to the end, so that a person who is truly in Christ will persevere and will not be lost, and that the warnings are the means by which God keeps his people in faith. Reformed teaching, often called Calvinist, states this as the perseverance of the saints and joins it to its account of election. The Westminster Confession (chapter 17), the standard of the Presbyterian Church in America and the Orthodox Presbyterian Church, and the Canons of Dort (Fifth Head), held by the Christian Reformed Church, add that a true believer can fall into grievous sin and lose the comfort of assurance for a time, but not totally or finally (Westminster Confession 17.1-3; Canons of Dort, Fifth Head, Articles 4-7), and the Canons name the gospel's warnings among the means God uses to preserve his people (Article 14). Baptist confessions state it: Southern Baptists in the Baptist Faith and Message 2000 (Article V) and Baptists of the 1689 London Confession (chapter 17). The Church of England's Article XVII speaks of those whom God has chosen in Christ as brought by him to everlasting salvation, and Anglican members differ among themselves. Its holders speak of people who leave the faith as people whose faith was not the saving kind, and not as saved people who lost their salvation, and they hold the warnings to be real and to be heeded by every believer. Assurance in this reading rests on God's promise and the Holy Spirit's witness, and is confirmed by the fruit of continuing faith (Westminster Confession 18.2; Canons of Dort, Fifth Head, Article 10; the 1689 London Confession, chapter 18).

readings.label: Eternal security: eternal life is given when a person believes and rests on Christ's work and God's faithfulness, so it is not lost
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the New Testament to say that eternal life is given when a person believes and is a present possession, held by what Christ has done and by God's faithfulness. The General Association of Regular Baptist Churches states the security of the saints in Article XIII of its Articles of Faith (all who are truly born again are kept by God the Father for Jesus Christ), and many Baptist and free-church readers state this as the security of the believer. Many of its holders use the phrase “once saved, always saved” for it; that is the popular form, and the phrase is not in the Baptist Faith and Message or the 1689 London Confession, which state the second reading. Some independent Charismatic churches hold it; the Assemblies of God disapproves of it by bylaw. Holders of this reading differ among themselves on whether every believer will keep believing and on what the warning passages address. Some say that a believer who lives in sin is disciplined by God and loses reward, not salvation.

communion.question: What does the Bible say about the Lord's Supper?
communion.intro: The Lord's Supper is the meal of bread and cup that Christ's followers keep in remembrance of him, as Jesus took bread and a cup at his last meal with his disciples, which Luke calls “this Passover” (Luke 22:15, 19-20; 1 Corinthians 11:23-26). It is also called communion or Holy Communion, the Eucharist, the breaking of bread (Acts 2:42), and, in the churches that use those names for the service, the Mass (Catholic) and the Divine Liturgy (Eastern Orthodox). Every church set out here keeps it, and they read the text differently on what the bread and the cup are. This page sets the main readings side by side, each in the words its holders use, and chooses none of them.

readings.label: The bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ: his words at the table say what they are
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take Jesus' words “This is My body” and “This is My blood of the covenant” (Matthew 26:26-28) to say what the bread and the cup are once they are set apart for the Supper. They take John 6, where he says his flesh is real food and his blood real drink, together with Paul's “participation in the blood of Christ” and “participation in the body of Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:16) and his warning about “sinning against the body and blood of the Lord” (11:27), to speak of the same gift. Catholic teaching, in the Council of Trent (Session 13, chapter 4) and the Catechism (1374-1376), holds that the whole substance of the bread is changed into Christ's body and the whole substance of the wine into his blood, so that the appearances of bread and wine remain, and it calls this change transubstantiation; the Catechism adds that the sacrifice of Christ and the sacrifice of the Eucharist are one single sacrifice (1367). Eastern Orthodox churches also confess that the bread and wine are changed into the body and blood of Christ. The Confession of Dositheus (1672) and the Longer Catechism of Philaret use the word “transubstantiated”, and each says the word is not to be taken to define the manner of the change (Dositheus, Decree 17; Longer Catechism, questions 339-340); the Orthodox Church in America's teaching on the Eucharist does not use the word and says the mystery defies analysis in rational and logical terms. The Catholic and Orthodox documents therefore agree that the gifts are the body and blood of Christ, and differ in how far the change is explained in terms of substance and appearance.

readings.label: The body and blood of Christ are truly present in, with and under the bread and wine, which remain bread and wine
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take Jesus' words “This is My body” literally and take the bread and wine to remain bread and wine: his body and blood are present and given with them, and every communicant receives them by mouth. Lutheran documents state this. The Augsburg Confession (Article X) teaches that the body and blood of Christ are truly present and are distributed to those who eat the Supper. The Small Catechism calls the sacrament the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ “under the bread and wine”, and the Large Catechism “in and under” them. The Epitome of the Formula of Concord (VII) teaches a sacramental union through which the bread and wine are truly his body and blood, and the Solid Declaration (VII) speaks of the body and blood as present in, under and with the bread. These documents reject transubstantiation (Smalcald Articles III, VI), the Mass as a sacrifice, and the teaching that the bread and wine are bare signs, tokens or memorials (Epitome VII). They say that those without faith also receive the body and blood, to their judgment (Epitome VII; 1 Corinthians 11:27-29), and that forgiveness is received by faith in the words “given and shed for you” (Small Catechism). They rest the presence on Christ's word and on his rule over all things (Epitome VII, citing Ephesians 1:22; Solid Declaration VII, citing Matthew 28:18).

readings.label: Christ is truly present to the believer and received by faith through the Holy Spirit: the bread and wine remain, and are the sign and pledge of what they give
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the New Testament to say that the believer truly shares in Christ's body and blood in the Supper, by the Holy Spirit and through faith, and take the bread and wine to remain bread and wine, called his body and blood as signs are named by what they give. The Heidelberg Catechism (questions 78-79) says the bread and wine are not changed into Christ's actual body and blood and are visible signs and pledges of them, while the believer shares in Christ by the Spirit. The Belgic Confession (Article 35) says Christ is in heaven and gives himself to believers through faith, who receive his body and blood by the Spirit and not by the mouth, in a manner beyond understanding. The Westminster Confession (29.5-7) says the elements remain bread and wine in substance and that worthy receivers feed on Christ crucified by faith, spiritually, Christ being present to their faith and not bodily in the elements. John Calvin (Institutes IV.17) speaks of a true and substantial communication of Christ's body and blood by the Spirit. The Anglican documents cited here state part of this reading in their own words: the Thirty-Nine Articles of the Church of England (Article XXVIII) say that to those who rightly, worthily and with faith receive, the bread broken is “a partaking of the Body of Christ” (a sharing in it), and that the body is received and eaten “after an heavenly and spiritual manner” (in a heavenly and spiritual way), with faith as the means; the Anglican Church in North America's catechism (question 133) says the body and blood are truly taken and received in the Lord's Supper by faith; neither document says in these words that the bread and wine remain or that they are a sign and pledge. Article XVIII of the Methodist Articles of Religion, held by the United Methodist Church, says that to those who receive rightly, worthily and with faith the bread broken is a partaking (a sharing) of the body of Christ, and that the body is given, taken and eaten after a heavenly and spiritual manner, faith being the means; it does not speak of the Holy Spirit or of the bread and wine remaining. The 1689 London Confession, held by some Baptist bodies, says worthy receivers spiritually receive and feed on Christ crucified, “really and indeed, yet not carnally” (that is, not in a bodily way) (30.7). These documents say that those without faith eat the sign and not Christ (Articles XXIX; Belgic 35; Westminster 29.8).

readings.label: A memorial: the bread and the cup remember and proclaim Christ's death, and the Supper is an ordinance that Christ commanded
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take Jesus' command “do this in remembrance of Me” and Paul's “you proclaim the Lord's death until He comes” to say what the Supper is for: believers remember and proclaim his death, and look ahead to his return, with a bread and a cup that stand for his body and blood. Documents that state this include the Baptist Faith and Message 2000 (Article VII), which calls the Supper “a symbolic act of obedience” in which members memorialize the death of the Redeemer and look to his second coming; the Articles of Faith of the General Association of Regular Baptist Churches (XV), which call it “the commemoration of His death until He come”; the Assemblies of God Statement of Fundamental Truths (6b), which calls it a symbol expressing the believer's sharing the divine nature of Christ, a memorial of his suffering and death and a prophecy of his second coming; and the Foursquare Declaration of Faith (IX), which calls the broken bread and the juice of the vine types of Christ's body and shed blood. The Dordrecht Confession (Article X) and the Schleitheim Confession (Article III) speak of the bread and cup in remembrance of his death and body and blood. The Mennonite Church USA confession (Article 12) calls the bread and cup signs and speaks of remembering Jesus' death and God's deliverance, and it also says that the supper re-presents (makes present again) the risen Christ in the church, whose members share in his body and blood; readers who stand near this reading differ among themselves on how Christ's presence is spoken of.

election.question: What does the Bible say about whether God chooses who will be saved?
election.intro: Christians read the Bible as saying that God chooses people and appoints them beforehand, and they ask whom God chooses, on what basis, and to what end. The New Testament speaks of the elect, of election and of being predestined, and the Hebrew Scriptures speak of God choosing a people. This page sets the main readings side by side, each in the words its holders use, and chooses none of them. How a person's own will answers God's is treated on a separate card, free will.

readings.label: God's choosing in view of faith: God foreknows who will trust in Christ and chooses them (what is called conditional election)
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the New Testament to say that God wants everyone to be saved, and that God chooses for glory those whom he foreknows will trust in Christ, so that the choosing answers faith and does not come before it. They read the “foreknew” of Romans 8:29 and the “foreknowledge” of 1 Peter 1:2 as naming what the choosing rests on. John Wesley's sermon On Predestination states this reading, with God's foreknowing causing nothing that he foresees, and many Wesleyan and Methodist members hold it; the Methodist Articles of Religion have no article on predestination, and Wesley's sermon Free Grace rejects the teaching that God appoints any person to condemnation before the world began. Holders of this reading add that God's grace goes before every human response and makes trust possible for everyone (what is called prevenient grace), so that faith is a gift received and no one's own achievement. The Confession of Dositheus (1672) speaks of God's predestining in view of how each would use the freedom God gave, with grace offered to all, and rejects election that rests on God's will alone; the Longer Catechism of Philaret teaches predestination as God's will to give all people the means to happiness, and cites the foreknowing of Romans 8:29. The Assemblies of God position paper on the assurance of salvation speaks of the predestination of the corporate body of Christ as of those God foreknew would respond to the Spirit's conviction, and some other Pentecostal and Charismatic members hold this reading. The Mennonite confession of 1995 does not speak of election or predestination; it says God offers salvation from sin to all people, and that a person's acceptance is a personal, voluntary decision. Many Lutherans in the older dogmatic tradition state election as made in view of faith; the Brief Statement of the Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod rejects that phrase. Many Baptist and free-church members hold this reading, and members of those traditions differ among themselves. The Catholic Church has not ruled between its schools on whether God's choosing rests on a foreseen response or on God's purpose alone; its Catechism (600) says God's plan of predestination includes each person's free response to his grace.

readings.label: God's choice before the foundation of the world, resting on his own purpose and not on anything foreseen in the chosen (what is called unconditional election)
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the New Testament to say that God chose those he saves before the world began, according to his own purpose, mercy and good pleasure, and not on account of anything foreseen in them, faith included, which God grants to those he chose. They read Israel's election as the pattern: God set his affection on a people for no merit of theirs. Reformed readers state this as the root of grace and of assurance. The Westminster Confession (chapter 3, held by the Presbyterian Church in America and the Orthodox Presbyterian Church) and the Canons of Dort (held by the Christian Reformed Church) also state that God passes over the rest and condemns them for their sin, which the Canons call reprobation, and both deny that God is the author of sin; some call this double predestination and others avoid the term, and the Westminster Confession says the doctrine is to be handled with special prudence and care. Lutheran readers hold that God chose those he saves in Christ, not on account of works or merit (Solid Declaration XI), and reject the teaching that God has ordained some to condemnation (Epitome XI). A Lutheran body, the Missouri Synod (1932), states that faith is not a condition before election. Catholic documents cited on this card say that God predestines no one to go to hell (Catechism 1037), and condemn the teaching that others are predestined by divine power to evil (Council of Trent, Session 6, canon 17). The Church of England's Article XVII states predestination to life as God's everlasting purpose, before the foundations of the world, to deliver those he chose in Christ; it says nothing of those passed over or of any foreseen faith. The Second London (1689) Baptist Confession, chapter 3, states this reading, including God's leaving others in their sin; the Baptist Faith and Message (2000) of the Southern Baptist Convention names election as God's gracious purpose without saying whether it rests on foreseen faith, so it is cited here and not credited. Many Baptist members hold this reading, and others in that tradition hold the first.

readings.label: God's choosing of a people in Christ: Christ is the Chosen One, Israel and the church are chosen peoples, and individuals share in the choosing by being in him (what is called corporate election)
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the New Testament to speak first of Christ as God's Chosen One, and then of a chosen people in him, so that the choosing is of a people and a person shares in it by being in Christ. They point out that the “us” and “you” of Ephesians 1 are plural, and that the Hebrew Scriptures speak of God choosing Israel as a people. Catholic teaching speaks of the Church as the new People of God, the chosen people of 1 Peter 2:9 (Lumen Gentium 9, the Second Vatican Council's document on the Church). The Dordrecht Confession (1632) calls the church “the chosen generation” (article VIII) and says that Christ, the Son of God, was “foreordained thereto before the foundation of the world” (article III). The Assemblies of God position paper on the assurance of salvation speaks of the predestination of the corporate body of Christ and sets it apart from predeterminism. Some Wesleyan and Methodist, Baptist and free-church members hold this reading, often together with the first, and members of those traditions differ among themselves. The Westminster Confession (3.5), the Canons of Dort (I.7) and Lutheran teaching (Epitome XI) place election in Christ, as the second reading does, but speak of a definite number of persons and not of a people; the Heidelberg Catechism (54) speaks of a community chosen for eternal life that the Son gathers from the human race. These are cited here and not credited with this reading. Christians who hold this reading differ on how the church's election stands beside Israel's, and Romans 11:28-29 is cited in that discussion.

faith-and-works.question: What does the Bible say about faith and works?
faith-and-works.intro: Christians read the New Testament as speaking of faith (trust in God and in Christ) and of works (what people do), and they join the two in different ways when they ask how a person comes to be right with God and how that person is finally saved. This page sets the main readings side by side, each in the words its holders use, and chooses none of them.

readings.label: Faith working through love: salvation is God's gift, and works done in God's grace belong to the life of the one he saves
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the New Testament to speak of a faith that is alive in love, and of works that God himself enables, as together belonging to being made righteous and to final salvation. Catholic teaching understands justification as more than the forgiveness of sins: God renews the person inwardly and makes them righteous (Council of Trent, Session 6, chapter 7), and speaks of works done in grace as bearing fruit and earning reward by that same grace. Catholic teaching holds that the first grace of justification cannot be merited by anyone (Catechism 2010). The Confession of Dositheus (1672) states justification as by faith working through love and does not accept faith alone as the whole account. Members of other traditions hold parts of this reading.

readings.label: By faith alone (what is called sola fide): God declares the believer righteous through faith in Christ, and good works follow as faith's fruit
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the New Testament to teach that a person stands righteous before God through faith in Christ and that works contribute nothing to that standing. Righteousness is credited to the believer from Christ (what is called imputation), and good works follow as the fruit and evidence of a faith that is alive. Lutheran and Reformed readers state this as the center of the gospel, each with their own account of the law. Southern Baptists (the Baptist Faith and Message 2000) and Baptists of the 1689 London Confession state justification by faith in their own confessions, and other Baptist and free-church readers hold it. The Church of England's Article XI states it. The Articles of Religion of the United Methodist Church state it in these words (Article IX: justified by faith only; Article X: good works are its fruit), and the Global Methodist Church names the Articles of Religion among its doctrinal standards; both add the account of holiness set out in the next reading. The Assemblies of God and the Foursquare Church state justification by faith with Christ's righteousness credited to the believer; the Foursquare Declaration (article VIII) teaches that it is God's will that believers be sanctified daily.

readings.label: Faith as obedient trust: believing and obeying are one response to God, and holiness of life belongs to the way of salvation
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the New Testament to speak of faith as trust that includes obedience, as in “the obedience that comes from faith” of Romans 1:5, so that following Christ is the shape faith takes in life and not an addition to it. Wesleyan and Methodist readers affirm that a person is justified by faith, faith being the only condition of justification (Wesley), with repentance and works necessary in another sense, for growth and for continuing in salvation; they hold that holiness of heart and life belongs to the continuing way of salvation, which a believer is called to keep, and from which, Wesleyan writers hold, a believer can fall away. The 1995 Mennonite confession speaks of following Christ in this life and walking in his way (Article 8), and refers to its Article 17, “Discipleship and the Christian Life”, for the teaching on discipleship. The 1995 Mennonite confession uses justification by faith as one name for salvation, says salvation is by grace and not by merit, and holds faith and faithful obedience to the covenant to be inseparable; Pentecostal and Charismatic readers, many of whose movements grew out of the holiness revivals, including the Azusa Street revival led by an African American preacher, share much of this. The Church of God (Cleveland) declaration speaks of sanctification as a work after the new birth, with holiness as the standard of life, while the Assemblies of God and the Foursquare Church state the second reading, with a call to lifelong obedience.

free-will.question: What does the Bible say about free will?
free-will.intro: Christians read the Bible as calling people to choose, to repent and to obey, and also as telling of God at work in the human will, and they join the two in different ways when they ask how free a person is in turning to God. The phrase 'free will' comes from later Christian and philosophical writing; the Bible's own words are about choosing, willing, drawing, hardening and being unwilling. This page sets the main readings side by side, each in the words its holders use, and chooses none of them.

readings.label: Free choice, helped by grace: the will is wounded and not lost, and a person freely cooperates with God or refuses him
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the text to speak throughout to people who can answer, as when God sets a choice before Israel or Christ stands at the door and knocks. Catholic teaching holds that sin has wounded the human will without destroying its freedom, that grace moves and prepares the will, and that a person freely assents to this grace or resists it (Council of Trent, Session 6, chapter 5 and canons 4-5). Within Catholic teaching, schools differ on how God's moving of the will and the will's own assent fit together, and the Church has not decided between them. Eastern Orthodox readers hold that the freedom given with the image of God remains, and speak of a lifelong cooperation of the human will with God's grace (what is called synergy). The Confession of Dositheus (1672) holds that the fallen keep free will, can by nature choose and work moral good, and need grace for the good that leads to salvation, where the regenerate can will, or not will, to cooperate with grace. The Church of England's Article X says that after the fall a person cannot turn and prepare himself by his own strength, and that God's grace goes before the will and then works with it; many Anglicans hold part of this reading, and Anglican members differ among themselves in how they put it. Catholic and Orthodox writers also cite Sirach 15:14, a book outside the Protestant canon and outside the text quoted on this page.

readings.label: A will that chooses as it wills, and wills as its nature leads (what is called the bondage of the will): God's working changes the will so that it turns to him
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the text to say that every person chooses what he most wants, and answers for it, and that fallen human nature leaves the will unwilling to turn to God until God works in it. Lutheran and Reformed readers hold this under names of their own (the bondage of the will, shared by both; and, among many Reformed readers and some Lutheran ones, compatibilism, the view that God's ordering of events and a person's own choosing are both true), with a shared concern that God alone be the source of a person's turning. Many Lutherans leave how God's working and a person's choosing fit together as a mystery the text does not explain. Lutheran teaching grants the will some liberty in civil matters and none in spiritual ones (Augsburg Confession XVIII), holds that the Spirit works faith through the Word and sacraments and is resisted by those who persistently reject the Word (Solid Declaration II), and the Missouri Synod's Brief Statement says that non-conversion is due to the person alone and that why some are converted and others not belongs to God's judgments. Lutheran and Reformed readers differ from each other on whether the Spirit's work can finally be resisted. Baptists of the 1689 London Confession (chapter 9) state this reading, and many Anglicans read the Church of England's Article X in this sense; other members of those traditions hold the others. How far sin reaches in a person, and whom God chooses, are the subject of other pages.

readings.label: Grace that frees every person to respond (what is called prevenient grace): the bound will is freed by God, and the answer is the person's own
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the text to say two things at once: that apart from God no one can come, and that God has given to everyone the grace that makes a response possible, so that the response is real and can be refused. Wesleyan and Methodist readers call this prevenient grace, grace that comes before any decision. Article VIII of the United Methodist Church's Articles of Religion says that no one can turn and prepare himself without the grace of God 'preventing us', and Wesley's sermons speak of this grace as given to every person. The Assemblies of God uses the term prevenient grace in its 2017 position paper on the assurance of salvation, and Pentecostal and Charismatic members mostly stand here. Among Baptists, the Free Will Baptist Treatise says that the power to believe is the gift of God and that believing is an act of the creature; the Baptist Faith and Message (2000) of the Southern Baptist Convention does not choose between this reading and the second, and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (chapter 9) states the second. Many other Baptist and free-church members hold this reading, including those who speak of the freedom of the will. Article X of the Church of England speaks of grace that goes before ('preventing') the will and then works with it, but does not say that this grace is given to everyone, so this page does not list the Anglican tradition among those holding this reading; Article X is listed under it as cited. The 1995 Mennonite confession says that human beings have free will though choice is limited, that by God's grace they can choose the bond of covenant relationship with God, that God offers salvation to all people, and that the Holy Spirit moves those who hear the good news to accept it while God brings them into right relationship without coercion, but it does not say that the grace that makes a response possible is given to everyone, so this page does not list the Anabaptist tradition among those holding this reading; the confession's Articles 7 and 8 are listed under it as cited.

human-nature.question: What does the Bible say about human nature?
human-nature.intro: Christians ask what a human being is: what a person is made of (body and soul, body, soul and spirit, or one living whole), what it means that people are made in God's image, and what Adam's fall changed in those who came after him. The readings below join these three matters in different ways, and the traditions do not always line up behind one of them. This page sets the readings side by side and chooses none. How far sin reaches into the will belongs to the card on total depravity and is left there.

readings.label: Body and soul made in God's image and called to union with him: the fall brought death and left a corrupted or wounded nature
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the text to describe a human being as body and soul together, made in God's image and made for union with God. Some early writers named three parts, body, soul and spirit. Catholic teaching names body and soul, and takes “spirit” to be the soul in its ordering to God, not a third part (Catechism 367). Catholic teaching speaks of original sin as the loss of the holiness and justice with which Adam was made, handed on by descent as a state and not as a personal act, leaving human nature wounded and not destroyed (Catechism 399, 404-405; Council of Trent, Session 5). The Orthodox Church in America, in a reply on its teaching pages, says that the consequences of the first sin, chiefly death, pass to all while only Adam and Eve are guilty of it. The Confession of Dositheus (1672) speaks of hereditary sin that flowed to Adam's posterity and of infants as subject to original sin, and the Longer Catechism (Q168) says all are born infected with sin and mortal. Many writers of the Eastern Orthodox tradition take “image” and “likeness” in Genesis 1:26 as two things: the image given, and the likeness to be grown into through a life of union with God (what is called theosis). None of the Orthodox documents cited here states this; the Longer Catechism (Q114) speaks only of the image, as righteousness and holiness of truth.

readings.label: Fallen in Adam: his sin brought condemnation and a corrupted nature on all his descendants (what is called original sin)
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take Romans 5 and the verses near it to say that Adam's sin brought condemnation and a corrupted nature on all who descend from him, so that each person is born under that condemnation and with that corruption. Lutheran readers, following the Formula of Concord (Solid Declaration, Article I), speak of the image as lost in its original righteousness and holiness, the person remaining God's creature. Reformed readers speak of the image as lost in the knowledge, righteousness and holiness it first had; Genesis 9:6 and James 3:9 are cited for a dignity that remains in the person, which Reformed writers state as the image remaining in a lesser sense. Lutheran readers confess this in the Augsburg Confession (Article II) and the Solid Declaration. Reformed readers confess it in the Westminster Confession (chapter 6) and the Canons of Dort (Third and Fourth Heads), and add that Adam stood for the whole human family (what is called federal headship), which the Westminster Confession (7.2), held by the Presbyterian Church in America and the Orthodox Presbyterian Church, sets in a covenant of works made with Adam and his posterity. Reformed confessions also speak of children who die in infancy: the Canons of Dort (I.17), held by the Christian Reformed Church, say that believing parents should not doubt the election and salvation of children God takes in infancy, and the Westminster Confession (10.3) says elect infants dying in infancy are regenerated and saved. Anglican readers hold the corruption of human nature in Article IX of the Church of England, which adds that it remains in the baptized and that every person born deserves God's wrath and damnation, with no condemnation for those who believe; Anglican members differ in how they state the guilt, and the catechism of the Anglican Church in North America (question 46) speaks of an inherited fallen and corrupted human nature. Wesleyan readers hold it in Article VII of the Articles of Religion of the United Methodist Church, and Wesleyan members differ in how they state the guilt; they hold also that Christ's work covers children who have not yet sinned (Confession of Faith, Article VI), and speak of regeneration as the renewal of man in righteousness and of believers as partakers of the divine nature (Confession of Faith, Article IX; 2 Peter 1:4, which the first reading also cites). Baptists of the 1689 London Confession (chapter 6) and the General Association of Regular Baptist Churches (Article VI) state the corruption of Adam's descendants and their guilt in him. The Foursquare Church's Declaration of Faith (Article III) states the corruption and guilt of Adam's descendants, and the Assemblies of God Statement of Fundamental Truths (Statement 4) names death, physical and spiritual, through Adam without further definition. Most in these traditions speak of a person as body and soul, and some as body, soul and spirit.

readings.label: One living person: soul, spirit, heart and body are the whole human being seen from different sides, and each person answers for his or her own sin
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take Genesis 2:7 to say that the man became a living being, not that a soul was placed in a body, and take “soul”, “spirit”, “heart” and “flesh” to name the whole person from different sides. Anabaptist readers hold that death and an inclination toward sin came to everyone through Adam while guilt belongs to a person's own sin, and that children are in God's care until they can answer for themselves; their members differ in how they put this. The Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995) says the sin of Adam and Eve affects all while each is held accountable for his or her own behavior (Article 7), says that infants and children are safe in the care of God, and uses the phrase “age of accountability” of baptism (Article 11); the Dordrecht Confession (1632, Article II) says death spread to all men, because all sinned (Romans 5:12). The Mennonite confession takes the image of God to belong to the whole person, made for relationship with God, with others and with creation, marred by sin and restored in Christ (Articles 6 and 7); it does not take up whether a person is two parts, three, or one. Many Baptist and free-church readers hold this account of the fall and speak of an age of accountability, before which a child is held not to answer for his or her own sin. The Southern Baptist Convention's Baptist Faith and Message (2000, Article III) says that Adam's posterity inherit a nature and an environment inclined toward sin and that they become transgressors, and are under condemnation, as soon as they are capable of moral action; it does not say how many parts a person has. Baptists of the 1689 London Confession hold the imputation of Adam's sin described in the previous reading. Baptist members differ on whether a person is two parts, three, or one. Wesleyan members differ: some hold the inherited guilt described in the previous reading, and others join this reading in holding that Christ's work covers children.

readings.label: Body, soul and spirit: the spirit is the part made to meet God, cut off at the fall and made alive again in Christ
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take 1 Thessalonians 5:23 to name three distinct parts of a person, and Hebrews 4:12 to show soul and spirit as divisible, the spirit being that by which a person knows and worships God. Many who hold it read Adam's fall as the death of the spirit toward God, and the new birth as that spirit made alive. The Assemblies of God Statement of Fundamental Truths (Statement 4) names spiritual death, which it describes as separation from God, and does not state how many parts a person has. Baptist and free-church members differ, many holding two parts. The first reading notes that some early writers named three parts.

sabbath.question: What does the Bible say about the Sabbath?
sabbath.intro: The Sabbath is the seventh day, a day of rest that the Bible roots in God's own rest at creation, gives as a commandment to Israel, and speaks of again in the sayings of Jesus and in the letters to the churches. Christians read these texts in different ways when they ask whether the command binds those who follow Christ, which day they keep, and what the New Testament means by rest. This page sets the main readings side by side, each in the words its holders use, and chooses none of them.

readings.label: The seventh day still kept: the Sabbath commandment stands for the people of God, and the day God blessed at creation is the day to keep
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the Sabbath to be older than Sinai, set apart by God at creation and written among the Ten Commandments, which they take Jesus to have upheld when He said He had not come to abolish the Law or the Prophets. They read the Gospels and Acts as showing Jesus, the women who followed Him and Paul keeping the seventh day, read the prophets as bringing foreigners and all mankind to the Sabbath, and read no verse as moving the day or ending the command. Seventh-day Adventist, Seventh Day Baptist and other seventh-day churches keep the seventh day, Saturday, as their day of rest and worship. No tradition listed on this page holds this reading as a whole, though individual members and congregations within some of them do; among Baptists, the Seventh Day Baptist General Conference keeps the seventh day, and its Statement of Belief describes that day as sacred time, a gift of God to all people, dating from creation and upheld in the Ten Commandments.

readings.label: The Sabbath fulfilled in Christ's rest: the weekly day pointed ahead, and the rest it pointed to is found in Christ and shared by those who believe
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take Paul to speak of the Sabbath, with feasts and new moons, as a shadow of things to come whose body belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:16-17), and take Hebrews to speak of a rest that believers enter now and finally. Catholic teaching, in its catechism, holds that Sunday fulfills the spiritual truth of the Jewish Sabbath and keeps the third commandment as a day of worship and rest, rooted in the Lord's resurrection and the apostolic age and bound by the Church's precept (Catechism 2174-2185); Eastern Orthodox teaching and worship keep Sunday as the day of resurrection and of the liturgy, within the whole year's cycle of feasts, and the Longer Catechism of Philaret, in treating the fourth commandment, says the Church keeps the first day of the week, the Day of the Resurrection, in the place of the seventh, with rest from worldly work on Sundays and greater holy days for worship and works of charity; Lutheran confessions hold that the commandment is kept in hearing God's word and that Sunday is kept by church order and not by divine command (Augsburg Confession XXVIII; Large Catechism, Third Commandment), without calling the day fulfilled in Christ, and the Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod's Brief Statement calls Sunday an ordinance of the Church under Christian liberty; Anabaptist readers speak of the rest that Christ gives and of all time as holy through him, and the 1995 Mennonite confession says that through Jesus all time is holy, that the church celebrates a day of holy rest, commonly the first day of the week, and that it is called to live by Sabbath justice at all times, drawing on the Sabbath year and the Jubilee, without saying that the weekly day is fulfilled or ended. John Calvin, a founder of the Reformed tradition (whose confessions state the next reading), takes the seventh day as a figure of spiritual rest whose ceremonial part ended with Christ; he says he does not cling so to the number seven as to bind the church to it, and rejects the view that the moral part remains in one day in seven, while keeping a set day for worship and good order (Institutes 2.8.28-34). Members of other traditions keep Sunday in ways close to this: Southern Baptists, in the Baptist Faith and Message (Article VIII), call the first day the Lord's Day, a Christian institution that commemorates the resurrection, with its activities left to each Christian's conscience, and the article does not use the word Sabbath; the Church of God (Cleveland) Practical Commitments call Sunday the Christian day of worship, commemorating the resurrection, and cite Colossians 2:16-17. The traditions named differ among themselves on whether any day of rest binds the conscience; what they share is the reading that the weekly day finds its fulfillment in Christ.

readings.label: The Lord's Day as the Christian Sabbath: the commandment stands, and the day of rest and worship now falls on the first day, the day of the resurrection
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the Sabbath to be a creation ordinance given before Sinai, and its commandment to belong to the moral law that Christ did not abolish, so that one day in seven is still set apart for rest and worship. They hold that the apostolic church met on the first day of the week, the day of Christ's resurrection, which Revelation calls the Lord's day, and that the Sabbath rhythm moved to that day under Christ (what is called Sabbatarianism, or the Christian Sabbath). The Westminster Standards, held by the Presbyterian Church in America and the Orthodox Presbyterian Church, state this at length, calling the first day the Christian Sabbath (Westminster Confession 21.7-8; Larger Catechism 115-121; Shorter Catechism 57-62). The Heidelberg Catechism (Question 103), held by the Christian Reformed Church, speaks of the day of rest and of the eternal Sabbath begun in this life, without the Westminster account of one day in seven; Reformed churches differ in how strictly the day is kept, and Calvin's Institutes, set beside the second reading, does not state this reading. The 1689 London Baptist Confession (chapter 22) states this strictly, as a positive-moral and perpetual commandment, and other Baptists keep the day less strictly. The Church of England's Second Book of Homilies, in its homily Of the Place and Time of Prayer, says Christians keep the first day, Sunday, as their Sabbath, their day of rest, and many Anglican members hold the reading in differing degrees of strictness. The United Methodist Church's Confession of Faith (Article XIV) says the Lord's Day is divinely ordained for worship and rest from unnecessary work, and does not use the word Sabbath; Wesleyan members hold the reading in differing degrees of strictness. Pentecostal and Charismatic congregations differ widely, some holding this reading and others the second.

speaking-in-tongues.question: What does the Bible say about speaking in tongues?
speaking-in-tongues.intro: Acts and 1 Corinthians tell of people who spoke in tongues, and Christians read them differently on three things: whether the gift is still given today, what the speech is (a human language, or speech no human community speaks), and how it belongs in the life of a church. This page sets the main readings side by side, each in the words its holders use, and chooses none of them.

readings.label: The gifts continue: speaking in tongues is a gift the Spirit still gives, for prayer and for the church
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the text to show tongues given at Pentecost, at Cornelius's house and at Ephesus, and then in the ordinary life of the church at Corinth, and they find nothing in it that sets a date on which the gift ends. They take the promise of Acts 2:39 and the Spirit's apportioning of gifts in 1 Corinthians 12 to reach every generation of believers. Pentecostal and Charismatic churches hold this as part of the Spirit's present work, with tongues used in private prayer (what is often called a prayer language) and in worship with interpretation; the Assemblies of God (Statement of Fundamental Truths 7 and 8) and the Church of God (Cleveland, Tennessee) teach that tongues is the first outward sign of being baptized in the Holy Spirit (what is called initial evidence), which the Assemblies of God teach as an experience distinct from and after the new birth, and not every Pentecostal and Charismatic church teaches it. On what the speech is, holders differ: some take the tongues of Acts 2 as human languages the speakers had not learned, and many take the tongues of Corinth as speech to God in a language no human community speaks (14:2). Members of other traditions, Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran, Reformed, Baptist and Methodist members among them, hold this reading in part, especially in charismatic renewal movements within their churches.

readings.label: The sign gifts have ended (what is called cessationism): tongues belonged to the apostles' age, as a sign
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the signs that marked the apostles (miracles, healing, tongues) to have been given to confirm the first preaching of the gospel and the founding of the church, and to have ended when that foundation was laid. They take the tongues of Acts 2 as human languages, each hearer hearing his own (2:6, 2:8), and the tongues of Corinth as the same gift, real languages that need an interpreter (14:10-11). Reformed and Baptist or free-church readers hold this, and their members differ over when the gifts ended and over how far the ending reaches, to healing and to prophecy as well as tongues. Among Reformed bodies, the Westminster Confession (the standard of the Presbyterian Church in America and the Orthodox Presbyterian Church) says that God's former ways of revealing his will have ceased (1.1), without naming tongues, and the Orthodox Presbyterian Church's 1978 General Assembly report, which is not a constitutional document, concludes that prophecy and tongues ceased with the close of the apostolic age. Among Baptists, the General Association of Regular Baptist Churches states in its Articles of Faith that the sign and revelatory gifts have fulfilled their purpose and are not applicable to the work of the Holy Spirit today, without naming tongues; the 1689 London Baptist Confession (chapter 1) says that the former ways of God's revealing his will have ceased, which concerns the completion of revelation, and is cited here without being credited as a statement on the sign gifts; the Baptist Faith and Message (Southern Baptist Convention, 2000) says the Spirit bestows gifts for service and does not mention tongues or their ending. Many who hold this reading affirm that the Spirit still works in believers, and that God still heals and answers prayer; what they hold to have ended is the gift of tongues and the other sign gifts. Members of both traditions are also found in the third reading.

readings.label: The Spirit may give the gift today, and whatever is practiced is tested, interpreted and ordered
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the text to say that the Spirit apportions gifts as He determines, that not every believer is given this one, that in the gathered church it needs interpretation and order, and that love comes first. They take the text to leave open whether, and until when, the gift is given, and they leave open whether the speech is a human language or another. Members of Catholic, Anglican, Reformed, Baptist and Wesleyan traditions are found here, each with their own emphasis: Catholic teaching, for example, speaks of the Spirit's gifts as given for the good of the church, to be received with thanksgiving and tested by those who lead it (Catechism 799-801 and 2003; Lumen Gentium 12), and the paragraphs cited do not take up whether tongues are given today, what the speech is, or interpretation and order in the gathered church. The Orthodox Church in America's teaching on prayer in the Spirit does not say the gifts have ended; it speaks of tongues as a gift Paul describes and that some believers have in our time, finds no evidence that the saints prayed in tongues or that it belonged to the church's liturgy, says it needs interpretation and order, and does not speak of testing it. Lutheran teaching, as the commission of the Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod stated it in 1972, holds that God does not necessarily give his church in all ages the same special gifts, rejects making tongues the primary or indispensable sign of baptism in the Spirit, teaches no second work of the Spirit beyond conversion, asks that claimed experiences be tested against God's word, and holds that the Spirit comes through the Word and sacraments; its conclusions do not say whether tongues are given today or take up interpretation and order in the congregation; Lutheran members within charismatic renewal differ. The Christian Reformed Church's position statement says Christ distributes his gifts when and where he wills, that genuine gifts may be exercised provided all things are done for edification and in good order, and that they are confirmed by the fruit of the Spirit; the Presbyterian Church in America's pastoral letter does not forbid tongues, rejects them as a means of new revelation or as an essential sign of Spirit baptism, and urges forbearance among those who differ. The Anglican Church in North America's catechism lists tongues and their interpretation among the gifts the Spirit distributes as he wills for the sake of the body of Christ, and does not take up testing or order. The United Methodist Church's guidelines on the charismatic movement call on the church to be aware of the Holy Spirit's manifestations today, describe the charismatic movement as stressing Spirit baptism without making tongues its initial evidence, and say that when tongues are spoken in a group there must be interpretation to ensure order; they do not say outright that tongues are given today, and they speak of discerning manifestations in general rather than of testing tongues. The 1995 Mennonite confession does not name tongues, interpretation or order; it says the Spirit is not silent in the present, that the church is built up by gifts given to each member, and that what is claimed is to be tested in the congregation against Christ and the Scriptures. Anabaptist congregations differ among themselves. Baptist members are found here too; the Baptist Faith and Message and the other Baptist documents read do not state this reading. Members of each of these traditions are also found in the first two readings.

total-depravity.question: What does the Bible say about what is called total depravity?
total-depravity.intro: Christians agree that sin is in every person and that rescue comes from God, and they ask how far sin reaches: whether it leaves the mind, the will and the image of God standing in some measure, and whether anyone can turn to God before God's grace has acted. This page sets the main readings side by side, each in the words its holders use, and chooses none of them. These are Christian readings; Jewish tradition reads the Hebrew Scriptures cited here differently, and does not teach inherited sin.

readings.label: Wounded and healed: the fall brought death and disorder to every person, the image of God remains, and grace heals the will and moves it
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the text to say that Adam's sin brought death and a disordered nature to all his descendants, and that human nature is wounded by it and not destroyed: the image of God, the conscience and the freedom of the will remain. Catholic teaching calls the inherited condition original sin, a state contracted by descent and not a personal act, and says that human nature has not been totally corrupted (Catechism 404-405). The Council of Trent teaches that free will was weakened and not extinguished (Session 6, chapter 1 and canon 5), that the first movement toward faith is itself given by grace, which a free will may assent to or refuse (Session 6, chapter 5), and that the view that all works done before justification are sins is to be rejected (Session 6, canon 7). Catholic teaching also holds that the inclination to sin that remains after baptism (what is called concupiscence) is not itself sin (Session 5, canon 5). The Orthodox Church in America, in a reply on its teaching pages, says that the consequences of the first sin, chiefly death, pass to all while only Adam and Eve are guilty of it. The Confession of Dositheus (1672) names what descended from the first man as the punishments that followed his transgression and not personal sins, and says that the fallen person keeps the created power to choose the good while unable of himself to do any work worthy of a Christian life. Orthodox readers speak of God's grace and the human will working together (what is called synergy). The two traditions differ over guilt and share the picture of a person wounded and healed. Some members of other traditions hold parts of this reading.

readings.label: Sin reaches every part of the person (what is called total depravity): left to itself no one seeks God or can turn to him, and God's grace gives the new heart
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the text to say that sin has touched every part of a person (the mind, the heart, the will), so that no one, apart from God's work in them, is able to seek God or to believe. “Total” names the reach of sin through the whole person and does not say that anyone is as evil as they could be. In this reading God's grace brings the new heart and faith; Reformed readers place the new birth before faith, and Lutheran readers hold that the Spirit works faith through the Word and sacraments. Reformed readers state it as total depravity or total inability, the first of what are called the five points of Calvinism; their churches state the teaching in the Westminster Confession (held by the Presbyterian Church in America and the Orthodox Presbyterian Church) and in the Canons of Dort (held by the Christian Reformed Church), in their own words. Lutheran readers speak of the bondage of the will in spiritual matters: the will is unable to turn to God and is not forced (Solid Declaration, Article II), and Lutherans differ from Reformed readers over whether grace can be resisted. Baptists of the 1689 London Confession state the same inability in their confession, and other Baptist and free-church readers who stand with the Reformed account hold it; others in those traditions hold the third reading. The Church of England's Articles IX and X say that human nature is far gone from original righteousness and that no one can turn and prepare himself by his own strength; Anglican members hold the reading in part, and they differ among themselves.

readings.label: Grace that goes before (what is called prevenient grace): sin has left no one able to turn to God unaided, and God's grace given to everyone makes a free response possible
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the text to say that sin has reached the whole person and left no one able to turn to God by their own power, and also that God's grace goes before every person and restores enough freedom to answer his call or to refuse it. Wesleyan and Methodist readers call this prevenient grace and place it as the first work of grace in a way of salvation that continues through justification and holiness; the Articles of Religion of the United Methodist Church (Article VIII) say that no one can do good works pleasing to God without the grace of God by Christ preventing us, and Wesley's sermons say that grace of this kind is given to every person. The Assemblies of God uses the term in its position paper on assurance. Many Baptist and free-church readers and other Pentecostal and Charismatic readers hold a similar account without always using the term. Members of each of these traditions differ among themselves, and some hold the second reading. Catholic members hold the grace that goes before in part, as Trent and the Catechism teach it, and place it with the first reading. Eastern Orthodox members hold the grace that goes before in part, as the Confession of Dositheus (1672) speaks of a preventing grace imparted to all and of use to those who are willing to cooperate with it, and place it with the first reading. Article X of the Church of England speaks of grace preventing us (going before us), but does not say that this grace is given to everyone, so this page does not list the Anglican tradition among those holding this reading; Article X is listed under it as cited. The 1995 Mennonite confession says that sinfulness affects the whole person and that people's own efforts alone are constantly corrupted, that God offers salvation to all people, and that the Holy Spirit moves those who hear the good news to accept it while God brings them into right relationship without coercion, but it does not say that the grace that makes an answer possible is given to everyone, so this page does not list the Anabaptist tradition among those holding this reading; the confession's Articles 7 and 8 are listed under it as cited.
